DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogy's begetting pattern and assigns the birth, "of whom", to Mary alone. I drop the broader claim that a mother's birth-verb by itself removes a father.

I grant the challenger's rows.
- Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist".
- Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John".
- Isaiah 8:3: "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son."
- Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain".

Each of these has a begetting father named beside the mother's verb. So the verb alone proves nothing, and I do not rest on it.

The kept limb has two footings.
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L3] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)") stands in both verses. In 1:2 it is active, "begat", for every man in the line. In 1:16 it passes to "was born", said "of whom", the woman. The verse stops saying "Joseph begat Jesus" at the one place where the pattern would require it.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:16, [L2] *gennaō* active then passive, and [L3] 1:2. Matthew keeps the begetting verb for the men down to Joseph and changes it for the child. The change is Matthew's own, and the reader must account for it.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Isaiah 8:3–4.** Isaiah 8:3 states "I went unto the prophetess", with [L2] *qārab* (H7126, "to approach", the margin's "approached"), and Genesis 4:1 states "Adam knew Eve his wife". Each father's act is in its verse. Matthew 1:18 gives instead "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". Matthew 1:25 says "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". The form is not the same.
- **Naming.** Luke 1:62, "And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called", does not make naming the father's act alone. Luke 1:31 gives it to Mary: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Isaiah 7:14 does the same: "a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel".
- **Matthew 1:1.** "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." [L2] *huios* (G5207, "a 'son'... used very widely of immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship") stands here and in Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David". The word covers remote and figurative kinship, so it does not by itself carry the begetting.

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name one source for what was conceived, "of the Holy Ghost". Neither names Joseph as a source; they give him the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Matthew 1:25 reaches back across the taking, and I grant that "until" bounds only the time after it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The margin reads "Gr. begotten".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands behind "conceived" in 1:20. The word that carries the begetting there is assigned to "the Holy Ghost".
- **[L3] Matthew 1:19:** "Joseph her husband, being a just [man]... was minded to put her away privily." A husband who had known her would have no ground to put her away. The angel's "for" gives the Holy Ghost as the ground for taking her, not Joseph himself.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:18 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] 1:19. The pregnancy is found "before they came together", and the one source given is the Holy Ghost. No row puts Joseph's knowing in that interval.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Matthew 1:24–25 and *paralambanō*.** "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L2] *paralambanō* (G3880, "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself") names the taking. [L2] *heōs* (G2193, "until") bounds the time after it. I accept both. They do not place a knowing before the taking, and Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together".
- **Matthew 1:19 and Deuteronomy 22:24.** "Joseph her husband" and "his neighbour's wife" make her his wife. That is not a row stating that he knew her.
- **Genesis 4:1.** "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". The knowing is stated in that verse. Matthew 1:18–25 states no such knowing for the conception.
- **1 John 5:1 and John 3:6.** 1 John 5:1 reads "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him". John 3:6 reads "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit". Both speak of a second, spiritual birth in people already born. In Matthew 1:20 the begotten thing is "in her" before birth, and "of the Holy Ghost" is its only stated source.
- **Romans 1:3, 2 Samuel 7:12, Acts 2:30.** I answer these under Link 5.

**LINK 3: NARROWED TO:** the answer to "How shall this be?" names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. I grant that *eperchomai* and *episkiazō* are not begetting verbs, so the link does not rest on them.

- **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- **[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") stands in 1:34, and *kaleō* (G2564, "to call") stands in 1:35.
- **[L3] Luke 1:31:** "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". Mary's "seeing I know not a man" is her present state, given as the reason the thing seems impossible. The angel's reply gives God's power and names no man.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:34–35, [L2] *ginōskō*, and [L3] 1:31. The question is "how", and the answer is "the Holy Ghost... the power of the Highest". The reply would be strange if it were Joseph's coming act.
- **The "therefore".** In 1:35 the "therefore also" stands in the same sentence as, and immediately after, the Holy Ghost clause. The title is tied to that clause, not only back to 1:32.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 1:8.** "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you". [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904, "to supervene, i.e. arrive") is a word of arrival. I grant it is used of the apostles' empowerment. I use it only as the verb the angel uses for the Holy Ghost, and it names no human act.
- **Luke 9:34.** "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them". I grant the use. [L3] Acts 5:15, "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them", shows the verb's range. The link does not depend on it.
- **Luke 1:32.** "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David". I grant that the title is given here before Mary's question. Verse 35 then gives the ground of the title.
- **1 Chronicles 28:6.** "Solomon thy son... for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father". That verse's covenant sonship is by choice ("I have chosen him"), and David is a named begetter in the same row. Luke 1:34–35 names no begetter, and the question asks how.
- **Luke 1:36.** "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren". The impossibility stated there is barrenness, "who was called barren". Luke 1:37, "For with God nothing shall be impossible", answers both. Mary's own problem is "seeing I know not a man".
- **Luke 1:31.** The conception is future, which is why "I know not a man" is the obstacle and the angel answers it.
- **Isaiah 7:16.** "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good". Matthew 1:22–23 sets Isaiah's sign as fulfilled in the birth. [L3] Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet". Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". The sign has two uses, and Isaiah 8:3 is the near one.

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Luke 3:23 sets the sonship of Joseph apart as "supposed", and John 6:42 puts "father" in the crowd's mouth. Luke 2:27 and 2:41 are the narrator's household naming, which I grant. I drop the claim that every "father" row reports opinion.

- **[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". The KJV sets this in a parenthesis, and the narrator does not give it in his own voice.
- **[L2]** *nomizō* (G3543, "to do by law (usage)... suppose, thing, be wont"). It is the verb of Luke 3:23. The KJV renders it "supposed" there, whatever its other uses.
- **[L3] John 6:42:** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" Those who say "whose father... we know" are the ones who cannot accept the claim of origin.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Luke 3:23, [L2] *nomizō* "supposed", and [L3] John 6:42. Joseph's fatherhood is reported as household and public reckoning, set against the child's own claim.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 16:13.** "where prayer was wont to be made". I grant that the verb names custom there, and context decides. In Luke 3:23 the KJV's own rendering is "supposed", and the parenthesis sets it apart.
- **Luke 2:27, 2:41, 2:33.** "the parents brought in the child Jesus", "his parents went to Jerusalem", and "Joseph and his mother marvelled". The narrator says "parents" in 2:27 and 2:41, which I grant as household naming. In 2:33 he says "Joseph and his mother", not "his father and mother".
- **John 1:45.** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph". This is Philip's report. It is a disciple's description in a verse about whom Moses wrote, and it does not state how the child was begotten.
- **Luke 2:48 and 2:49.** "thy father and I" is Mary's household speech, with [L2] *patēr* (G3962, "a 'father' (literally or figuratively, near or more remote)"). The child's reply is "my Father's business" (2:49). The reply sets another Father against "thy father". 1 Chronicles 28:6 has David as the named begetter beside the choosing God. In Luke 2:48–49 the child's answer corrects the title in the same exchange.

**LINK 5: NARROWED TO:** Joseph's house gives the child his standing in David's house, through the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Mary is of David's house, because no quoted row states it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "he called his name JESUS".
- **[L3] Luke 2:4:** "because he was of the house and lineage of David". Deuteronomy 25:6 gives a case of reckoning by name: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother [which is] dead".
- **[L2]** *shem* (H8034, "an appellation, as a mark or memorial of individuality") stands in Deuteronomy 25:6.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:20 and 1:25 and [L3] Luke 2:4 and Deuteronomy 25:6. The son of David takes the wife, names the child, and the child is reckoned in his house. The child's descent is not a begetting by him.

Answers to the presses:
- **Luke 1:27 and Luke 2:4.** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David". [L2] *anēr* (G435, "a man... husband"). I grant that the house is Joseph's in Luke.
- **Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:5.** Elisabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron". I grant that this says nothing of Mary's house.
- **Galatians 4:4.** "made of a woman, made under the law". I grant that it names the mother. Job 14:1, "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days", is a general statement.
- **Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:10.** "made of the seed of David according to the flesh", "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne", and "he was yet in the loins of his father". [L2] *sperma* (G4690, "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')"). I do not say how David's seed reached the child, and the link no longer claims it.

**LINK 6: NARROWED TO:** the stated source of what was conceived in Mary is the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20), and Matthew 1:16 does not say that Joseph begat Jesus. I drop the claim that the flesh came through Mary's side. My conclusion that Christ had no human biological father rests on Link 1's narrowed limb, Link 2's narrowed limb and Link 3's narrowed limb, not on a descent through the woman.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands in both verses.
- **[L3] Luke 1:35:** "that holy thing which shall be born of thee".
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:16 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] Luke 1:35.

Answers to the presses:
- **Hebrews 7:14, 7:5, 7:9 and Numbers 1:18.** "our Lord sprang out of Juda"; "though they come out of the loins of Abraham"; "Levi also... payed tithes in Abraham"; "by the house of their fathers". [L2] *yalad* (H3205, "to bear young; causatively, to beget"). These show that tribal descent runs by fathers' houses. They do not show that Joseph was the begetter, and the narrowed link no longer claims descent through the woman.
- **Ezra 2:61–62.** "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name". I grant the register case.
- **2 Samuel 7:12, Psalms 132:11 and Acts 2:30.** "which shall proceed out of thy bowels", "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne", and "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh". I grant that these name David's body. I do not say how it reached the child.
- **Matthew 1:20 and Romans 1:4.** "Joseph, thou son of David" and "declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness". Matthew 1:20 also carries "of the Holy Ghost" as the one source.
- **Genesis 4:1 and Matthew 1:19.** "Adam knew Eve his wife" and "Joseph her husband". The first states the knowing. The second states the husband's title.

# LINK ROUND: Challenger's answers to the six premises

The defender pressed nineteen verses against my chain. Each is quoted below under the premise it was pressed against, and the fit is shown with its layers.

---

## LINK 1: SUPPORTED

The premise: *"So the loins of David reach Christ through a line of fathers."*

**[L1] Acts 2:30:** "Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne". The oath sets Christ in David's loins, according to the flesh.

**[L2]** *osphys* (G3751, "the loin... internally (by extension) procreative power") stands in Acts 2:30. The same word stands in Hebrews 7:10, "For he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." In 2 Samuel 7:12, "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels", the word for seed is *zera'* (H2233, "seed... posterity").

**[L3]**
- Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda". The epistle uses the loins-of-the-father word in this same chapter.
- Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers". The word *'ab* (H1, "father") stands in that phrase.
- Luke 2:4 says Joseph "was of the house and lineage of David".
- Matthew 1:20 has the angel say "Joseph, thou son of David".

**[L4]** The oath puts the seed in David's loins [L1]. "Loins" is the father's procreative word [L2]. The tribe is "evident" by the house of the fathers. The one man the text places in David's house and lineage is Joseph [L3]. So the loins of David reach Christ through a line of fathers.

**The presses answered:**

- **Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;"
  - *gennaō* (G1080) is glossed "properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother". In 1:16 the passive with "of whom" uses that extension: it names the mother.
  - The defender has already granted that a mother's birth-verb "alone proves nothing" (his narrowed Link 1).
  - The same verse names Joseph "the husband of Mary". The line of "begat" in Matthew 1:2 runs to him.
  - Matthew 1:1 heads that line: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David". The word there is *genesis* (G1078, "nativity").
  - So Matthew 1:16 carries the line of fathers to the husband and names the mother. It fits the link.
- **Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli".

**LINK 1: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogy's begetting pattern and assigns the birth, "of whom", to Mary alone. I drop the broader claim that a mother's birth-verb by itself removes a father.

- Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain".

Each of these has a begetting father named beside the mother's verb. So the verb alone proves nothing, and I do not rest on it.

The kept limb has two footings.
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L3] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)") stands in both verses. In 1:2 it is active, "begat", for every man in the line. In 1:16 it passes to "was born", said "of whom", the woman. The verse stops saying "Joseph begat Jesus" at the one place where the pattern would require it.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:16, [L2] *gennaō* active then passive, and [L3] 1:2. Matthew keeps the begetting verb for the men down to Joseph and changes it for the child. The change is Matthew's own, and the reader must account for it.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Isaiah 8:3–4.** Isaiah 8:3 states "I went unto the prophetess", with [L2] *qārab* (H7126, "to approach", the margin's "approached"), and Genesis 4:1 states "Adam knew Eve his wife". Each father's act is in its verse. Matthew 1:18 gives instead "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". Matthew 1:25 says "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". The form is not the same.

Luke 1:31 gives it to Mary: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". [L2] *huios* (G5207, "a 'son'... used very widely of immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship") stands here and in Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David". The word covers remote and figurative kinship, so it does not by itself carry the begetting.

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name one source for what was conceived, "of the Holy Ghost". Neither names Joseph as a source; they give him the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Matthew 1:25 reaches back across the taking, and I grant that "until" bounds only the time after it.

[L2] *paralambanō* (G3880, "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself") names the taking. [L2] *heōs* (G2193, "until") bounds the time after it. I accept both. They do not place a knowing before the taking, and Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together".

**LINK 3: NARROWED TO:** the answer to "How shall this be?" names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. I grant that *eperchomai* and *episkiazō* are not begetting verbs, so the link does not rest on them.

Answers to the other presses:

- **Luke 1:36.** "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren". The impossibility stated there is barrenness, "who was called barren". Luke 1:37, "For with God nothing shall be impossible", answers both. Mary's own problem is "seeing I know not a man".
- **Luke 1:31.** The conception is future, which is why "I know not a man" is the obstacle and the angel answers it.
- **Isaiah 7:16.** "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good". Matthew 1:22–23 sets Isaiah's sign as fulfilled in the birth. [L3] Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet". Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". The sign has two uses, and Isaiah 8:3 is the near one.

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Luke 3:23 sets the sonship of Joseph apart as "supposed", and John 6:42 puts "father" in the crowd's mouth. Luke 2:27 and 2:41 are the narrator's household naming, which I grant. I drop the claim that every "father" row reports opinion.

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 breaks the genealogy's begetting pattern and assigns the birth, "of whom", to Mary alone. I drop the broader claim that a mother's birth-verb by itself removes a father.

I grant the challenger's rows.
- Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist".
- Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John".
- Isaiah 8:3: "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son."
- Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain".

Each of these has a begetting father named beside the mother's verb. So the verb alone proves nothing, and I do not rest on it.

The kept limb has two footings.
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L3] Matthew 1:2:** "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)") stands in both verses. In 1:2 it is active, "begat", for every man in the line. In 1:16 it passes to "was born", said "of whom", the woman. The verse stops saying "Joseph begat Jesus" at the one place where the pattern would require it.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:16, [L2] *gennaō* active then passive, and [L3] 1:2. Matthew keeps the begetting verb for the men down to Joseph and changes it for the child. The change is Matthew's own, and the reader must account for it.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Isaiah 8:3–4.** Isaiah 8:3 states "I went unto the prophetess", with [L2] *qārab* (H7126, "to approach", the margin's "approached"), and Genesis 4:1 states "Adam knew Eve his wife". Each father's act is in its verse. Matthew 1:18 gives instead "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost". Matthew 1:25 says "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". The form is not the same.
- **Naming.** Luke 1:62, "And they made signs to his father, how he would have him called", does not make naming the father's act alone. Luke 1:31 gives it to Mary: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Isaiah 7:14 does the same: "a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel".
- **Matthew 1:1.** "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." [L2] *huios* (G5207, "a 'son'... used very widely of immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship") stands here and in Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David". The word covers remote and figurative kinship, so it does not by itself carry the begetting.

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name one source for what was conceived, "of the Holy Ghost". Neither names Joseph as a source; they give him the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Matthew 1:25 reaches back across the taking, and I grant that "until" bounds only the time after it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The margin reads "Gr. begotten".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands behind "conceived" in 1:20. The word that carries the begetting there is assigned to "the Holy Ghost".
- **[L3] Matthew 1:19:** "Joseph her husband, being a just [man]... was minded to put her away privily." A husband who had known her would have no ground to put her away. The angel's "for" gives the Holy Ghost as the ground for taking her, not Joseph himself.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:18 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] 1:19. The pregnancy is found "before they came together", and the one source given is the Holy Ghost. No row puts Joseph's knowing in that interval.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Matthew 1:24–25 and *paralambanō*.** "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L2] *paralambanō* (G3880, "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself") names the taking. [L2] *heōs* (G2193, "until") bounds the time after it. I accept both. They do not place a knowing before the taking, and Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together".
- **Matthew 1:19 and Deuteronomy 22:24.** "Joseph her husband" and "his neighbour's wife" make her his wife. That is not a row stating that he knew her.
- **Genesis 4:1.** "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". The knowing is stated in that verse. Matthew 1:18–25 states no such knowing for the conception.
- **1 John 5:1 and John 3:6.** 1 John 5:1 reads "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him". John 3:6 reads "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit". Both speak of a second, spiritual birth in people already born. In Matthew 1:20 the begotten thing is "in her" before birth, and "of the Holy Ghost" is its only stated source.
- **Romans 1:3, 2 Samuel 7:12, Acts 2:30.** I answer these under Link 5.

**LINK 3: NARROWED TO:** the answer to "How shall this be?" names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. I grant that *eperchomai* and *episkiazō* are not begetting verbs, so the link does not rest on them.

- **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- **[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") stands in 1:34, and *kaleō* (G2564, "to call") stands in 1:35.
- **[L3] Luke 1:31:** "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". Mary's "seeing I know not a man" is her present state, given as the reason the thing seems impossible. The angel's reply gives God's power and names no man.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:34–35, [L2] *ginōskō*, and [L3] 1:31. The question is "how", and the answer is "the Holy Ghost... the power of the Highest". The reply would be strange if it were Joseph's coming act.
- **The "therefore".** In 1:35 the "therefore also" stands in the same sentence as, and immediately after, the Holy Ghost clause. The title is tied to that clause, not only back to 1:32.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 1:8.** "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you". [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904, "to supervene, i.e. arrive") is a word of arrival. I grant it is used of the apostles' empowerment. I use it only as the verb the angel uses for the Holy Ghost, and it names no human act.
- **Luke 9:34.** "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them". I grant the use. [L3] Acts 5:15, "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them", shows the verb's range. The link does not depend on it.
- **Luke 1:32.** "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David". I grant that the title is given here before Mary's question. Verse 35 then gives the ground of the title.
- **1 Chronicles 28:6.** "Solomon thy son... for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father". That verse's covenant sonship is by choice ("I have chosen him"), and David is a named begetter in the same row. Luke 1:34–35 names no begetter, and the question asks how.
- **Luke 1:36.** "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren". The impossibility stated there is barrenness, "who was called barren". Luke 1:37, "For with God nothing shall be impossible", answers both. Mary's own problem is "seeing I know not a man".
- **Luke 1:31.** The conception is future, which is why "I know not a man" is the obstacle and the angel answers it.
- **Isaiah 7:16.** "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good". Matthew 1:22–23 sets Isaiah's sign as fulfilled in the birth. [L3] Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet". Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". The sign has two uses, and Isaiah 8:3 is the near one.

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Luke 3:23 sets the sonship of Joseph apart as "supposed", and John 6:42 puts "father" in the crowd's mouth. Luke 2:27 and 2:41 are the narrator's household naming, which I grant. I drop the claim that every "father" row reports opinion.

- **[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". The KJV sets this in a parenthesis, and the narrator does not give it in his own voice.
- **[L2]** *nomizō* (G3543, "to do by law (usage)... suppose, thing, be wont"). It is the verb of Luke 3:23. The KJV renders it "supposed" there, whatever its other uses.
- **[L3] John 6:42:** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" Those who say "whose father... we know" are the ones who cannot accept the claim of origin.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Luke 3:23, [L2] *nomizō* "supposed", and [L3] John 6:42. Joseph's fatherhood is reported as household and public reckoning, set against the child's own claim.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 16:13.** "where prayer was wont to be made". I grant that the verb names custom there, and context decides. In Luke 3:23 the KJV's own rendering is "supposed", and the parenthesis sets it apart.
- **Luke 2:27, 2:41, 2:33.** "the parents brought in the child Jesus", "his parents went to Jerusalem", and "Joseph and his mother marvelled". The narrator says "parents" in 2:27 and 2:41, which I grant as household naming. In 2:33 he says "Joseph and his mother", not "his father and mother".
- **John 1:45.** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph". This is Philip's report. It is a disciple's description in a verse about whom Moses wrote, and it does not state how the child was begotten.
- **Luke 2:48 and 2:49.** "thy father and I" is Mary's household speech, with [L2] *patēr* (G3962, "a 'father' (literally or figuratively, near or more remote)"). The child's reply is "my Father's business" (2:49). The reply sets another Father against "thy father". 1 Chronicles 28:6 has David as the named begetter beside the choosing God. In Luke 2:48–49 the child's answer corrects the title in the same exchange.

**LINK 5: NARROWED TO:** Joseph's house gives the child his standing in David's house, through the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Mary is of David's house, because no quoted row states it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "he called his name JESUS".
- **[L3] Luke 2:4:** "because he was of the house and lineage of David". Deuteronomy 25:6 gives a case of reckoning by name: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother [which is] dead".
- **[L2]** *shem* (H8034, "an appellation, as a mark or memorial of individuality") stands in Deuteronomy 25:6.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:20 and 1:25 and [L3] Luke 2:4 and Deuteronomy 25:6. The son of David takes the wife, names the child, and the child is reckoned in his house. The child's descent is not a begetting by him.

Answers to the presses:
- **Luke 1:27 and Luke 2:4.** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David". [L2] *anēr* (G435, "a man... husband"). I grant that the house is Joseph's in Luke.
- **Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:5.** Elisabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron". I grant that this says nothing of Mary's house.
- **Galatians 4:4.** "made of a woman, made under the law". I grant that it names the mother. Job 14:1, "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days", is a general statement.
- **Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:10.** "made of the seed of David according to the flesh", "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne", and "he was yet in the loins of his father". [L2] *sperma* (G4690, "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')"). I do not say how David's seed reached the child, and the link no longer claims it.

**LINK 6: NARROWED TO:** the stated source of what was conceived in Mary is the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20), and Matthew 1:16 does not say that Joseph begat Jesus. I drop the claim that the flesh came through Mary's side. My conclusion that Christ had no human biological father rests on Link 1's narrowed limb, Link 2's narrowed limb and Link 3's narrowed limb, not on a descent through the woman.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands in both verses.
- **[L3] Luke 1:35:** "that holy thing which shall be born of thee".
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:16 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] Luke 1:35.

Answers to the presses:
- **Hebrews 7:14, 7:5, 7:9 and Numbers 1:18.** "our Lord sprang out of Juda"; "though they come out of the loins of Abraham"; "Levi also... payed tithes in Abraham"; "by the house of their fathers". [L2] *yalad* (H3205, "to bear young; causatively, to beget"). These show that tribal descent runs by fathers' houses. They do not show that Joseph was the begetter, and the narrowed link no longer claims descent through the woman.
- **Ezra 2:61–62.** "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name". I grant the register case.
- **2 Samuel 7:12, Psalms 132:11 and Acts 2:30.** "which shall proceed out of thy bowels", "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne", and "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh". I grant that these name David's body. I do not say how it reached the child.
- **Matthew 1:20 and Romans 1:4.** "Joseph, thou son of David" and "declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness". Matthew 1:20 also carries "of the Holy Ghost" as the one source.
- **Genesis 4:1 and Matthew 1:19.** "Adam knew Eve his wife" and "Joseph her husband". The first states the knowing. The second states the husband's title.

Luke 1:31 gives it to Mary: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS". Isaiah 7:14 does the same: "a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel".
- **Matthew 1:1.** "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." [L2] *huios* (G5207, "a 'son'... used very widely of immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship") stands here and in Matthew 1:20, "Joseph, thou son of David". The word covers remote and figurative kinship, so it does not by itself carry the begetting.

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name one source for what was conceived, "of the Holy Ghost". Neither names Joseph as a source; they give him the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Matthew 1:25 reaches back across the taking, and I grant that "until" bounds only the time after it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:18:** "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost". The margin reads "Gr. begotten".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands behind "conceived" in 1:20. The word that carries the begetting there is assigned to "the Holy Ghost".
- **[L3] Matthew 1:19:** "Joseph her husband, being a just [man]... was minded to put her away privily." A husband who had known her would have no ground to put her away. The angel's "for" gives the Holy Ghost as the ground for taking her, not Joseph himself.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:18 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] 1:19. The pregnancy is found "before they came together", and the one source given is the Holy Ghost. No row puts Joseph's knowing in that interval.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Matthew 1:24–25 and *paralambanō*.** "took unto him his wife: And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son". [L2] *paralambanō* (G3880, "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself") names the taking. [L2] *heōs* (G2193, "until") bounds the time after it. I accept both. They do not place a knowing before the taking, and Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together".
- **Matthew 1:19 and Deuteronomy 22:24.** "Joseph her husband" and "his neighbour's wife" make her his wife. That is not a row stating that he knew her.
- **Genesis 4:1.** "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived". The knowing is stated in that verse. Matthew 1:18–25 states no such knowing for the conception.
- **1 John 5:1 and John 3:6.** 1 John 5:1 reads "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him". John 3:6 reads "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit". Both speak of a second, spiritual birth in people already born. In Matthew 1:20 the begotten thing is "in her" before birth, and "of the Holy Ghost" is its only stated source.
- **Romans 1:3, 2 Samuel 7:12, Acts 2:30.** I answer these under Link 5.

**LINK 3: NARROWED TO:** the answer to "How shall this be?" names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, and names no man. I grant that *eperchomai* and *episkiazō* are not begetting verbs, so the link does not rest on them.

- **[L1] Luke 1:34:** "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- **[L1] Luke 1:35:** "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") stands in 1:34, and *kaleō* (G2564, "to call") stands in 1:35.
- **[L3] Luke 1:31:** "thou shalt conceive in thy womb". Mary's "seeing I know not a man" is her present state, given as the reason the thing seems impossible. The angel's reply gives God's power and names no man.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] 1:34–35, [L2] *ginōskō*, and [L3] 1:31. The question is "how", and the answer is "the Holy Ghost... the power of the Highest". The reply would be strange if it were Joseph's coming act.
- **The "therefore".** In 1:35 the "therefore also" stands in the same sentence as, and immediately after, the Holy Ghost clause. The title is tied to that clause, not only back to 1:32.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 1:8.** "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you". [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904, "to supervene, i.e. arrive") is a word of arrival. I grant it is used of the apostles' empowerment. I use it only as the verb the angel uses for the Holy Ghost, and it names no human act.
- **Luke 9:34.** "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them". I grant the use. [L3] Acts 5:15, "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them", shows the verb's range. The link does not depend on it.
- **Luke 1:32.** "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David". I grant that the title is given here before Mary's question. Verse 35 then gives the ground of the title.
- **1 Chronicles 28:6.** "Solomon thy son... for I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father". That verse's covenant sonship is by choice ("I have chosen him"), and David is a named begetter in the same row. Luke 1:34–35 names no begetter, and the question asks how.
- **Luke 1:36.** "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... who was called barren". The impossibility stated there is barrenness, "who was called barren". Luke 1:37, "For with God nothing shall be impossible", answers both. Mary's own problem is "seeing I know not a man".
- **Luke 1:31.** The conception is future, which is why "I know not a man" is the obstacle and the angel answers it.
- **Isaiah 7:16.** "For before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good". Matthew 1:22–23 sets Isaiah's sign as fulfilled in the birth. [L3] Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet". Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son". The sign has two uses, and Isaiah 8:3 is the near one.

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Luke 3:23 sets the sonship of Joseph apart as "supposed", and John 6:42 puts "father" in the crowd's mouth. Luke 2:27 and 2:41 are the narrator's household naming, which I grant. I drop the claim that every "father" row reports opinion.

- **[L1] Luke 3:23:** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph". The KJV sets this in a parenthesis, and the narrator does not give it in his own voice.
- **[L2]** *nomizō* (G3543, "to do by law (usage)... suppose, thing, be wont"). It is the verb of Luke 3:23. The KJV renders it "supposed" there, whatever its other uses.
- **[L3] John 6:42:** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?" Those who say "whose father... we know" are the ones who cannot accept the claim of origin.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Luke 3:23, [L2] *nomizō* "supposed", and [L3] John 6:42. Joseph's fatherhood is reported as household and public reckoning, set against the child's own claim.

Answers to the other presses:
- **Acts 16:13.** "where prayer was wont to be made". I grant that the verb names custom there, and context decides. In Luke 3:23 the KJV's own rendering is "supposed", and the parenthesis sets it apart.
- **Luke 2:27, 2:41, 2:33.** "the parents brought in the child Jesus", "his parents went to Jerusalem", and "Joseph and his mother marvelled". The narrator says "parents" in 2:27 and 2:41, which I grant as household naming. In 2:33 he says "Joseph and his mother", not "his father and mother".
- **John 1:45.** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph". This is Philip's report. It is a disciple's description in a verse about whom Moses wrote, and it does not state how the child was begotten.
- **Luke 2:48 and 2:49.** "thy father and I" is Mary's household speech, with [L2] *patēr* (G3962, "a 'father' (literally or figuratively, near or more remote)"). The child's reply is "my Father's business" (2:49). The reply sets another Father against "thy father". 1 Chronicles 28:6 has David as the named begetter beside the choosing God. In Luke 2:48–49 the child's answer corrects the title in the same exchange.

**LINK 5: NARROWED TO:** Joseph's house gives the child his standing in David's house, through the taking and the naming. I drop the claim that Mary is of David's house, because no quoted row states it.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:25:** "he called his name JESUS".
- **[L3] Luke 2:4:** "because he was of the house and lineage of David". Deuteronomy 25:6 gives a case of reckoning by name: "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother [which is] dead".
- **[L2]** *shem* (H8034, "an appellation, as a mark or memorial of individuality") stands in Deuteronomy 25:6.
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:20 and 1:25 and [L3] Luke 2:4 and Deuteronomy 25:6. The son of David takes the wife, names the child, and the child is reckoned in his house. The child's descent is not a begetting by him.

Answers to the presses:
- **Luke 1:27 and Luke 2:4.** "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David". [L2] *anēr* (G435, "a man... husband"). I grant that the house is Joseph's in Luke.
- **Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:5.** Elisabeth is "of the daughters of Aaron". I grant that this says nothing of Mary's house.
- **Galatians 4:4.** "made of a woman, made under the law". I grant that it names the mother. Job 14:1, "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days", is a general statement.
- **Romans 1:3, Acts 2:30 and Hebrews 7:10.** "made of the seed of David according to the flesh", "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne", and "he was yet in the loins of his father". [L2] *sperma* (G4690, "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')"). I do not say how David's seed reached the child, and the link no longer claims it.

**LINK 6: NARROWED TO:** the stated source of what was conceived in Mary is the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20), and Matthew 1:16 does not say that Joseph begat Jesus. I drop the claim that the flesh came through Mary's side. My conclusion that Christ had no human biological father rests on Link 1's narrowed limb, Link 2's narrowed limb and Link 3's narrowed limb, not on a descent through the woman.

- **[L1] Matthew 1:20:** "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost".
- **[L1] Matthew 1:16:** "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus".
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate") stands in both verses.
- **[L3] Luke 1:35:** "that holy thing which shall be born of thee".
- **[L4]** This rests on [L1] Matthew 1:16 and 1:20, [L2] *gennaō*, and [L3] Luke 1:35.

Answers to the presses:
- **Hebrews 7:14, 7:5, 7:9 and Numbers 1:18.** "our Lord sprang out of Juda"; "though they come out of the loins of Abraham"; "Levi also... payed tithes in Abraham"; "by the house of their fathers". [L2] *yalad* (H3205, "to bear young; causatively, to beget"). These show that tribal descent runs by fathers' houses. They do not show that Joseph was the begetter, and the narrowed link no longer claims descent through the woman.
- **Ezra 2:61–62.** "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name". I grant the register case.
- **2 Samuel 7:12, Psalms 132:11 and Acts 2:30.** "which shall proceed out of thy bowels", "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne", and "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh". I grant that these name David's body. I do not say how it reached the child.
- **Matthew 1:20 and Romans 1:4.** "Joseph, thou son of David" and "declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness". Matthew 1:20 also carries "of the Holy Ghost" as the one source.
- **Genesis 4:1 and Matthew 1:19.** "Adam knew Eve his wife" and "Joseph her husband". The first states the knowing. The second states the husband's title.

## CHALLENGER'S UNSUPPORTED-L4 PREMISES

1. The inference that the line of fathers reaches the child through Joseph's begetting, which props the Hebrews 7:14 objection. Challenger's words: "So the loins of David reach Christ through a line of fathers."
PRESSED WITH:
Matthew 1:16 "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." -- MEANS: the active "begat" runs to Joseph, and the child is "born" of the woman, so the verse does not close the line by a father's begetting -- [L2] gennaō (G1080, "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother)") | [L3] Matthew 1:2 "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren;"

Matthew 1:19 "was minded to put her away privily" -- MEANS: a husband who had known her would have no ground to put her away -- [L2] thelō (G2309, "to determine... i.e. choose or prefer... intend") | [L3] Matthew 1:20 "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife"

PRESSED WITH:

Matthew 1:19 "Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." -- MEANS: the man who had the title "husband" is minded to put her away, which fits no prior knowing -- [L2] paralambanō (G3880, "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself") in Matthew 1:24 | [L3] Matthew 1:18 "before they came together"

DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 3, LINK ROUND

## LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate, properly of the father") is the verb in every "begat" of the line. At Matthew 1:16 the "of whom" is the feminine singular relative *hēs* ("of whom," pointing to Mary alone). It is not the masculine, which would point back to Joseph.
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac." Matthew 1:3: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar." Matthew 1:5: "Booz begat Obed of Ruth."
- **[L4]** Footing: the L1 verse, the L2 feminine "of whom," and the L3 pattern.
  1. In Matthew 1:2-16 every father is the subject of "begat."
  2. At the one place where Jesus comes into the line, the subject is not a man. The relative turns to Mary alone.
  3. So the line names Joseph "the husband of Mary" and stops short of "Joseph begat Jesus."

*Presses answered*
- Matthew 1:3, "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar," and Matthew 1:5, "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab." In both the man is the subject of "begat" beside the woman. That is the contrast. Where a father begets, the text writes him as subject. At 1:16 it does not.
- Matthew 11:11, "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist." I grant that a bare passive proves no absence. The link rests on the contrast of subjects. Luke 1:13 also puts the father in the row: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son." Matthew 1:21 reads "she shall bring forth a son," with no "thee."
- Matthew 1:19, "Then Joseph her husband," and Matthew 1:20, "Mary thy wife." *anēr* (G435, "a man, husband") gives Joseph the title of husband. Matthew 1:16 and 1:19 give that title and no row writes "father."

**LINK 2: SUPPORTED**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
- **[L2]** *gennaō* (G1080, "to procreate"), the margin's "begotten," is the verb Matthew gave the fathers in 1:2-16. Here its source is "the Holy Ghost."
- **[L3]** Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- **[L4]** Footing: L1, L2, L3. The thing "in her" has as its source the Holy Ghost, in the verb that elsewhere in the chapter has a man as source. Of the thing conceived, no row names a man.

*Presses answered*
- 1 John 5:1, "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God," and John 1:13, "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." John 1:13 itself sets "of God" against "the will of man." It is said of believers after faith. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 say "of the Holy Ghost" of "that which is conceived in her," at the conception and before the birth.
- John 3:6, "that which is born of the Spirit is spirit." It names a birth of spirit in believers. It does not read as the conception of a child "found with child" (Matthew 1:18).
- Romans 1:3, "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." *sperma* (G4690, "seed, offspring") is descent from David. Hebrews 2:16 uses the same word: "he took on [him] the seed of Abraham." Romans 1:3 names David's seed and does not name Joseph as begetter. Hebrews 10:5 says of the body: "a body hast thou prepared me."
- 1 Chronicles 28:6, "I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father," and 2 Samuel 7:14, "I will be his father, and he shall be my son." In both the sonship rests on God's choice of one already born, and the human father is called "thy son's" father in the verse. Luke 1:35 gives a cause at the conception, "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee." The angel does not say "thy son" to Joseph (Matthew 1:21).

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED**

- **[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- **[L2]** *boulomai* (G1014, "to be minded") and *apolyō* (G630, "to put away, divorce") stand in Matthew 1:19. *paradeigmatizō* (G3856, "to expose to infamy") names what he would not do.
- **[L3]** Deuteronomy 24:1: "because he hath found some uncleanness in her... let him write her a bill of divorcement." Deuteronomy 22:23: "a man find her in the city, and lie with her." Matthew 1:25: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- **[L4]** Footing: L1, L2, L3.
  1. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together."
  2. Matthew 1:25 puts the not-knowing from the taking to the birth.
  3. No row leaves a time before the birth when they came together. So the pregnancy found is not one he caused.
  4. Deuteronomy 24:1 gives the ground for divorce as "uncleanness found," not a wife carrying her husband's child.
  5. The angel's "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20) answers a fear about taking her. A father would have no such fear.

*Presses answered*
- Matthew 1:19 states two grounds, justice and unwillingness to expose. Both fit mine. *dikaios* (G1342, "just, equitable") is why he would not take a wife found with child before they came together, and unwillingness to expose is why he would do it privily.
- Deuteronomy 22:24, "his neighbour's wife," and Matthew 1:24, "took unto him his wife." I grant that the betrothed was a wife in law. Deuteronomy 22:23 treats lying with her as a separate act after betrothal, and Deuteronomy 20:7 treats taking as a further step after betrothal. Betrothed as wife does not say "came together."
- Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." *yada* (H3045, "to know, lie with") there joins the knowing to the conception. Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 deny the knowing before the birth. Matthew 1:20 gives the Holy Ghost as source.
- Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb," is future. Luke 1:34, "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" is asked of that future conception, and Luke 1:35 answers with the Holy Ghost in place of a man.

**LINK 4: SUPPORTED**

- **[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."
- **[L2]** *almah* (H5959, the word behind the KJV's "virgin") is the word the KJV prints "virgin" here. The KJV prints the Greek in Matthew 1:23, "a virgin shall be with child," with *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin"), and Matthew 1:25 says she was not known till the birth.
- **[L3]** Isaiah 8:3: "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz." Isaiah 7:14: "shall call his name Immanuel." Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled."
- **[L4]** Footing: L1, L2, L3. Matthew states the sign as fulfilled in a woman found with child "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18). A "sign" that falls in the very condition Matthew states is not an ordinary conception by a husband.

*Presses answered*
- Isaiah 8:3, "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son." That child is told "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz," and the sign child's name in Isaiah 7:14 is Immanuel. Isaiah 8:8, "O Immanuel," addresses the land, not that son. So the two are not shown to be one child.
- Isaiah 7:16, "before the child shall know to refuse the evil." I take it as the nearer sign to Ahaz. Matthew 1:22-23 applies the verse to the conception of Jesus, and Matthew states the fulfilment.
- Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:15, "he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb." Elisabeth's sign is that she "was called barren." Luke 1:13 says "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son," with "thee." Luke 1:35 says "born of thee," and Matthew 1:21 says "she shall bring forth a son," with no "thee." John is *filled* in the womb. Jesus is *begotten* of the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20, the margin). The two verbs differ.
- Acts 1:8, "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you," and Luke 9:34, "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them." In both the persons already exist. In Luke 1:35 the thing "which shall be born of thee" does not yet exist.
- Luke 1:32 and Luke 1:35 together: "therefore also" (*dio kai*) in 1:35 stands in the same verse as the two clauses before it, "come upon thee... overshadow thee," and gives their result.

**LINK 5: NARROWED TO:** (A) a child not begotten by Joseph is not of Coniah's seed by the flesh; (B) his flesh is of David's seed through Mary. I drop the house-by-Heli reading as a stated fact. No row names Mary's father.

- **[L1]** Jeremiah 22:30: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah."
- **[L3] for A:** Matthew 1:12: "Jechonias begat Salathiel." Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary." Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David." Matthew 1:20: "of the Holy Ghost."

## LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
- [L2] *gennaō* (G1080), "to procreate (properly, of the father…)". The KJV's own margin renders the verb "begotten", so the begetting is assigned to the Holy Ghost.
- [L3] Luke 1:34–35: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The answer is "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost," and this is "before they came together."
- [L4] Mary asks how, and the answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, never a man. Matthew 1:18 dates the source before any coming together. So the conception was not from a male human parent.

Answers to the pressed witnesses:
- **Matthew 1:20** ("Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife"). [L2] *phobeō* (G5399), "to be alarmed". The angel's word answers Joseph's alarm by naming the Holy Ghost as source. If Joseph were the source, the verse would give him no reason for alarm. [L2] *huios* (G5207) is "son" of "immediate, remote or figuratively" kinship. It marks Joseph's descent and does not say he begat.
- **1 John 5:1** ("is born of God"). This is the figure of the same verb, "to regenerate", said of men already born. Matthew 1:20 speaks of "that which is conceived in her", a conception in a womb. The verb is the same and the object differs.
- **John 1:13** ("not of the will of man, but of God"). [L2] *anēr* (G435), "a man… husband". The verse itself sets "of God" against a man's will. That is the contrast Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 apply to the child, literally.
- **1 John 3:9** ("his seed remaineth in him"). The seed here is God's, in a believer, and is not a man's. It is a figure and gives David's seed to no one.
- **John 3:6** ("That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit"). This states two births of one man. Luke 1:35 names one thing "born of thee" and calls it "that holy thing".
- **Romans 1:3 and 1:4.** I take both halves. [L3] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman". [L2] *ginomai* (G1096), "used with great latitude", is the verb of both verses. [L2] *sperma* (G4690) is "seed… by implication, offspring". That is David's offspring, and it does not name a father's act at the last step.
- **Acts 2:30, Hebrews 7:10 and Matthew 1:2.** I agree that loins reach down a line. [L3] Hebrews 7:9: "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham." That is a reach across many generations, with mothers in the line. Acts 2:30 requires David's descent. It does not require that the last step be a male begetter. In Acts 2:30 the one who "would raise up Christ" is God.

---

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 turns the line from "begat" to "of whom was born", ending the begetting at Joseph "the husband of Mary" and naming Mary as the one of whom Jesus was born. I drop the words "sole parent."

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L3] Matthew 1:15: "Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob." Every earlier step of the line takes "begat". The last step does not, and it is introduced as a different mode: Matthew 1:18, "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise."
- [L4] The verb changes where Joseph is named "husband", and the passive "was born" is carried by Mary alone. The line ends at Joseph without a begetting of Jesus.

Answers:
- **Matthew 1:2** ("Abraham begat Isaac"). It is a line of begats up to Matthew 1:16, where the verb for Jesus differs. Hebrews 7:5 is the loins of a forefather, as I answered at Link 1.
- **Genesis 4:1 and H3045 *yada*** ("to know"). The knowing is the husband's. Matthew 1:25 says "knew her not till she had brought forth", and Luke 1:34 puts Mary's "I know not a man" before the conception.
- **Matthew 1:20.** Joseph is called son of David, and the angel's next clause is "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **Matthew 1:25 and Luke 1:13, 1:62** (the naming). Luke 1:31 gives Mary the naming: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS." Genesis 4:25 says of Eve, "and called his name Seth." So naming is no mark of begetting. Joseph's naming (Matthew 1:21, 1:25) follows his "took unto him his wife" (Matthew 1:24). That is his act of receiving, and it places the child in his house in law.

---

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L2] *heōs* (G2193), "until". It bounds the not-knowing at the birth.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" is dated "before they came together."
- [L3] Luke 1:27 and 1:34: "a virgin espoused to a man". Mary says "seeing I know not a man", at the visit within the espousal.
- [L4] The conception is "found" at Matthew 1:18 and called "conceived" by the angel at Matthew 1:20, both before the taking of Matthew 1:24. The challenger's own order is: espousal, finding, taking. So the child was already conceived when Joseph took her, and the not-knowing from the taking to the birth was not the cause. Mary's own words in the espousal say she knew no man.

Answers:
- **Matthew 1:24 and Deuteronomy 20:7.** The taking is later than the finding. That strengthens this link.
- **Matthew 1:19** ("was minded to put her away privily"). [L2] *thelō* (G2309), "to determine". The grounds given are just and unwilling to make her a public example. [L3] Deuteronomy 22:23: "a damsel that is a virgin be betrothed unto an husband, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her". The law's case is a betrothed damsel with another man. Joseph's plan to put her away fits a man who knew he was not the cause. A husband who knew her would have no such plan.
- **Deuteronomy 22:24** ("his neighbour's wife"). Granted, a betrothed damsel is a wife in law. That is Joseph's legal standing and says nothing of knowing.
- **Genesis 4:1.** The text's means of conceiving is the husband knowing, and Luke 1:35 gives a different means for this one conception.
- **Luke 2:5** ("Mary his espoused wife, being great with child"). She is still "espoused" at the journey. Matthew 1:25 says he knew her not until the birth. They agree.

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Isaiah 7:14 ("Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son"), as applied to the conception of Jesus by Matthew 1:22–23. I drop Genesis 4:25, Job 14:1 and Matthew 11:11 as witnesses to a source. I granted they are said of sons with fathers.

- [L3] Isaiah 7:11, 7:14: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above," and "the Lord himself shall give you a sign".
- [L4] The KJV itself applies Isaiah 7:14 to "all this", the conception of Matthew 1:18–25. The sign is a virgin who conceives, and that is not a conception by a husband.

Answers:
- **Isaiah 7:16** (the land forsaken of both kings) and **Isaiah 8:3–4, 8:8.** [L3] Isaiah 8:3: "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz". The child of Isaiah 8:3 is named something else. Isaiah 8:8's "O Immanuel" is the name addressed to the land. Matthew 1:22 gives the KJV's fulfilment to the conception of Jesus.
- **Genesis 3:15, Genesis 4:25, Job 14:1, Matthew 11:11.** Dropped as above. I do not rest on them.
- **Matthew 1:20** (Joseph son of David). The chapter that applies Isaiah 7:14 also names the husband. That is the husband of Matthew 1:16, and Matthew 1:20 names the begetting as of the Holy Ghost.

**LINK 5: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".
- [L2] *nomizō* (G3543), "to do by law (usage)", hence to reckon or deem. The passive "was supposed" names what was reckoned by the people. That is the link's own words, "opinion or legal reckoning".

Answers:

- **Numbers 1:18** ("by the house of their fathers") and **Ezra 2:59, 2:62.** The register is by father's house. Joseph takes Mary and names the child (Matthew 1:20–21, 1:24–25). That puts Jesus in his house in law, which is the reckoning "supposed" names.
- **Luke 2:48.** Mary speaks of "thy father" in the household's way. Luke 2:49 gives the child's answer.
- **Luke 2:27, 2:41** ("the parents", "his parents"). The same narrator writes "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33, Luke 2:43) and "the young child and his mother" (Matthew 2:13, 2:20). The narration carries the household word.
- **Luke 2:51** ("subject unto them"). It states a household and does not state a begetting.
- **1 Chronicles 28:6** ("I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father"). [L2] *bachar* (H977), "to try, i.e. select". Solomon is God's son by choice. Luke 1:35 gives another ground: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The "therefore" follows the Holy Ghost clause in the same verse.

**LINK 6: SUPPORTED**

The same word says "his father" of Abraham in Hebrews 7:10, which the challenger granted is a forefather. The promise is spoken to Mary of the son she will bear, and Mary's question follows at Luke 1:34. Luke 1:27 places Joseph of David's house and does not state Mary's. Luke 1:35 answers "how".
- **Luke 1:35.** [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904) and [L3] Acts 1:8, "the Holy Ghost is come upon you". I grant the verb is empowerment. Here the thing empowered is a conception. Here it is joined to "the power of the Highest" and to "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". "Called" names the title. The conception is stated at Luke 1:31 before it.

- **Hebrews 7:14.** [L2] *sprang out* is a rising out of a stock, and the tribe is the line's. [L3] Hebrews 7:5 says all the sons of Levi "come out of the loins of Abraham", through many mothers. The flesh line through Mary is inference.

## LINK ROUND

**LINK 1: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
- [L2] *gennaō* (G1080), "to procreate (properly, of the father…)". The KJV's own margin renders the verb "begotten", so the begetting is assigned to the Holy Ghost.
- [L3] Luke 1:34–35: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" The answer is "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost," and this is "before they came together."
- [L4] Mary asks how, and the answer names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, never a man. Matthew 1:18 dates the source before any coming together. So the conception was not from a male human parent.

Answers to the pressed witnesses:
- **Matthew 1:20** ("Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife"). [L2] *phobeō* (G5399), "to be alarmed". The angel's word answers Joseph's alarm by naming the Holy Ghost as source. If Joseph were the source, the verse would give him no reason for alarm. [L2] *huios* (G5207) is "son" of "immediate, remote or figuratively" kinship. It marks Joseph's descent and does not say he begat.
- **1 John 5:1** ("is born of God"). This is the figure of the same verb, "to regenerate", said of men already born. Matthew 1:20 speaks of "that which is conceived in her", a conception in a womb. The verb is the same and the object differs.
- **John 1:13** ("not of the will of man, but of God"). [L2] *anēr* (G435), "a man… husband". The verse itself sets "of God" against a man's will. That is the contrast Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 apply to the child, literally.
- **1 John 3:9** ("his seed remaineth in him"). The seed here is God's, in a believer, and is not a man's. It is a figure and gives David's seed to no one.
- **John 3:6** ("That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit"). This states two births of one man. Luke 1:35 names one thing "born of thee" and calls it "that holy thing".
- **Romans 1:3 and 1:4.** I take both halves. [L3] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman". [L2] *ginomai* (G1096), "used with great latitude", is the verb of both verses. [L2] *sperma* (G4690) is "seed… by implication, offspring". That is David's offspring, and it does not name a father's act at the last step.
- **Acts 2:30, Hebrews 7:10 and Matthew 1:2.** I agree that loins reach down a line. [L3] Hebrews 7:9: "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham." That is a reach across many generations, with mothers in the line. Acts 2:30 requires David's descent. It does not require that the last step be a male begetter. In Acts 2:30 the one who "would raise up Christ" is God.

---

**LINK 2: NARROWED TO:** Matthew 1:16 turns the line from "begat" to "of whom was born", ending the begetting at Joseph "the husband of Mary" and naming Mary as the one of whom Jesus was born. I drop the words "sole parent."

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L3] Matthew 1:15: "Eleazar begat Matthan; and Matthan begat Jacob." Every earlier step of the line takes "begat". The last step does not, and it is introduced as a different mode: Matthew 1:18, "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise."
- [L4] The verb changes where Joseph is named "husband", and the passive "was born" is carried by Mary alone. The line ends at Joseph without a begetting of Jesus.

Answers:
- **Matthew 1:2** ("Abraham begat Isaac"). It is a line of begats up to Matthew 1:16, where the verb for Jesus differs. Hebrews 7:5 is the loins of a forefather, as I answered at Link 1.
- **Genesis 4:1 and H3045 *yada*** ("to know"). The knowing is the husband's. Matthew 1:25 says "knew her not till she had brought forth", and Luke 1:34 puts Mary's "I know not a man" before the conception.
- **Matthew 1:20.** Joseph is called son of David, and the angel's next clause is "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- **Matthew 1:25 and Luke 1:13, 1:62** (the naming). Luke 1:31 gives Mary the naming: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS." Genesis 4:25 says of Eve, "and called his name Seth." So naming is no mark of begetting. Joseph's naming (Matthew 1:21, 1:25) follows his "took unto him his wife" (Matthew 1:24). That is his act of receiving, and it places the child in his house in law.

---

**LINK 3: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L2] *heōs* (G2193), "until". It bounds the not-knowing at the birth.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost" is dated "before they came together."
- [L3] Luke 1:27 and 1:34: "a virgin espoused to a man". Mary says "seeing I know not a man", at the visit within the espousal.
- [L4] The conception is "found" at Matthew 1:18 and called "conceived" by the angel at Matthew 1:20, both before the taking of Matthew 1:24. The challenger's own order is: espousal, finding, taking. So the child was already conceived when Joseph took her, and the not-knowing from the taking to the birth was not the cause. Mary's own words in the espousal say she knew no man.

Answers:
- **Matthew 1:24 and Deuteronomy 20:7.** The taking is later than the finding. That strengthens this link.
- **Matthew 1:19** ("was minded to put her away privily"). [L2] *thelō* (G2309), "to determine". The grounds given are just and unwilling to make her a public example. [L3] Deuteronomy 22:23: "a damsel that is a virgin be betrothed unto an husband, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her". The law's case is a betrothed damsel with another man. Joseph's plan to put her away fits a man who knew he was not the cause. A husband who knew her would have no such plan.
- **Deuteronomy 22:24** ("his neighbour's wife"). Granted, a betrothed damsel is a wife in law. That is Joseph's legal standing and says nothing of knowing.
- **Genesis 4:1.** The text's means of conceiving is the husband knowing, and Luke 1:35 gives a different means for this one conception.
- **Luke 2:5** ("Mary his espoused wife, being great with child"). She is still "espoused" at the journey. Matthew 1:25 says he knew her not until the birth. They agree.

---

**LINK 4: NARROWED TO:** Isaiah 7:14 ("Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son"), as applied to the conception of Jesus by Matthew 1:22–23. I drop Genesis 4:25, Job 14:1 and Matthew 11:11 as witnesses to a source. I granted they are said of sons with fathers.

Footing:
- [L1] Matthew 1:22–23: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet… Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
- [L2] *parthenos* (G3933), "a virgin". Matthew 1:23 puts the word on the conception of Jesus.
- [L3] Isaiah 7:11, 7:14: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above," and "the Lord himself shall give you a sign".
- [L4] The KJV itself applies Isaiah 7:14 to "all this", the conception of Matthew 1:18–25. The sign is a virgin who conceives, and that is not a conception by a husband.

Answers:
- **Isaiah 7:16** (the land forsaken of both kings) and **Isaiah 8:3–4, 8:8.** [L3] Isaiah 8:3: "Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz". The child of Isaiah 8:3 is named something else. Isaiah 8:8's "O Immanuel" is the name addressed to the land. Matthew 1:22 gives the KJV's fulfilment to the conception of Jesus.
- **Genesis 3:15, Genesis 4:25, Job 14:1, Matthew 11:11.** Dropped as above. I do not rest on them.
- **Matthew 1:20** (Joseph son of David). The chapter that applies Isaiah 7:14 also names the husband. That is the husband of Matthew 1:16, and Matthew 1:20 names the begetting as of the Holy Ghost.

**LINK 5: SUPPORTED**

Footing:
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph".
- [L2] *nomizō* (G3543), "to do by law (usage)", hence to reckon or deem. The passive "was supposed" names what was reckoned by the people. That is the link's own words, "opinion or legal reckoning".
- [L3] Luke 2:48–49: "behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." The child answers "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Mary's "thy father" is answered in the next verse by another Father.
- [L3] Luke 1:34–35, where the same writer has already told the reader the source.
- [L4] Luke 1:35 gives the source, Luke 2:49 answers "thy father" with "my Father's", and Luke 3:23 sets "as was supposed" in parenthesis beside "Jesus himself". So the Joseph reckoning is the reckoning of others.

Answers:
- **Acts 16:13** ("wont to be made"). It is the same passive, a custom thought to hold. That fits "reckoned by usage".
- **Numbers 1:18** ("by the house of their fathers") and **Ezra 2:59, 2:62.** The register is by father's house. Joseph takes Mary and names the child (Matthew 1:20–21, 1:24–25). That puts Jesus in his house in law, which is the reckoning "supposed" names.
- **Luke 2:48.** Mary speaks of "thy father" in the household's way. Luke 2:49 gives the child's answer.
- **Luke 2:27, 2:41** ("the parents", "his parents"). The same narrator writes "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33, Luke 2:43) and "the young child and his mother" (Matthew 2:13, 2:20). The narration carries the household word.
- **Luke 2:51** ("subject unto them"). It states a household and does not state a begetting.
- **1 Chronicles 28:6** ("I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father"). [L2] *bachar* (H977), "to try, i.e. select". Solomon is God's son by choice. Luke 1:35 gives another ground: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The "therefore" follows the Holy Ghost clause in the same verse.

**LINK 6: SUPPORTED**

Footing:

- [L3] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman". [L2] *ginomai* (G1096) is the verb also of Romans 1:3, so the flesh comes by the woman.
- [L3] Matthew 1:18, 1:20 and Luke 1:34, as at Link 1.
- [L4] The conception is in Mary (Luke 1:31) by the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20), in answer to "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34). The flesh is of Mary's womb (Luke 1:35). The KJV does not state Mary's tribe in so many words. That limb is my inference, footed on Luke 1:32 (below) and on Romans 1:3's "seed of David".

Answers:
- **Luke 1:32** ("the throne of his father David"). [L2] *patēr* (G3962) is "a 'father' (literally or figuratively, near or more remote)". The same word says "his father" of Abraham in Hebrews 7:10, which the challenger granted is a forefather. The promise is spoken to Mary of the son she will bear, and Mary's question follows at Luke 1:34. Luke 1:27 places Joseph of David's house and does not state Mary's. Luke 1:35 answers "how".
- **Luke 1:35.** [L2] *eperchomai* (G1904) and [L3] Acts 1:8, "the Holy Ghost is come upon you". I grant the verb is empowerment. Here the thing empowered is a conception. [L3] Luke 1:34 asks how Mary shall conceive, knowing "not a man". [L3] Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15 use "overshadowed" of presence. Here it is joined to "the power of the Highest" and to "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". "Called" names the title. The conception is stated at Luke 1:31 before it.
- **2 Samuel 7:12 and Psalms 132:11.** "thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels" is first said of the next son (2 Samuel 7:14, "If he commit iniquity"). It names a line, and the line reaches Jesus by descent, as Hebrews 7:9 shows for Levi.
- **Acts 2:30, Romans 1:3.** As at Link 1. David's fruit is the line. Galatians 4:4 puts the making on the woman.
- **Hebrews 7:14.** [L2] *sprang out* is a rising out of a stock, and the tribe is the line's. [L3] Hebrews 7:5 says all the sons of Levi "come out of the loins of Abraham", through many mothers. [L3] Luke 1:5 and 1:36 show Mary's cousin Elisabeth "of the daughters of Aaron", so mothers' kin cross tribes. The register is the legal line through Joseph (Matthew 1:20–21, 1:24–25). The flesh line through Mary is inference.
- **Luke 2:4** (Joseph "of the house and lineage of David"). It names Joseph's house and does not name a begetting.
